metric.dependency_simplicity.description: Assessment of language-level dependency semantics for Swift: how the language itself expresses and resolves module/package dependencies, independent of package-manager maturity (which is Ecosystem).
observations: Swift has a first-class module system (`import Module`) with no header files, no preprocessor-based inclusion, and no implicit global namespace pollution, unlike C/C++.
Access control (`public`/`internal`/`fileprivate`/`private`) and module boundaries are enforced by the compiler, giving strong, simple dependency isolation semantics at the language level.

Standard library and Foundation are cleanly separated; a pure Swift program (as in the micro benchmark set, e.g. mb00.swift-mb11.swift) can be written using only the Swift standard library with zero external dependencies, and this is idiomatic, not exceptional.

Swift Package Manager's manifest (Package.swift) is itself written in Swift, so dependency declarations are type-checked language constructs rather than an ad hoc external DSL -- a language-level dependency-simplicity property distinct from the ecosystem's package registry maturity.

However, on non-Apple platforms Swift's dependency on the Swift runtime and (for many programs) Foundation/Dispatch introduces platform-conditional imports (`#if canImport(Foundation)`), adding minor complexity not present in a language with a fully platform-independent standard library.
Reviewed micro benchmark sources (mb01-mb11) import only `Foundation` or no external module, consistent with low intrinsic dependency surface for typical numeric/string workloads.
metric.dependency_simplicity.score_rationale: Scored 78/100: strong module system and language-native manifest reduce dependency complexity considerably versus C/C++, but conditional-import patterns needed for full cross-platform Foundation parity and the coupling to the Swift runtime prevent a top score.

metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.description: Assessment of Swift's language design portability: is the language specification and core semantics platform-neutral, separate from realized platform support breadth (an Ecosystem concern).
observations: Swift's core language (types, generics, protocols, concurrency model with async/await, ARC memory model) is specified without platform-specific semantics and is implemented via LLVM, enabling in principle cross-platform code generation.

In practice, large parts of the standard runtime experience (Objective-C interop, many Foundation behaviors, availability annotations like @available(iOS ...)) are historically tied to Apple platforms, and the language itself carries first-class syntax (`@available`, `#if os(iOS)`) whose most common use cases are Apple-platform-specific -- this is a language design choice that embeds platform-conditional constructs directly into source rather than isolating them at a build-config layer.

ABI stability (frozen since Swift 5) was designed primarily around Apple's platform ABI; on Linux/Windows the ABI story is separate and less unified, reflecting platform-coupled design decisions rather than a neutral single ABI target.

Value types, protocol-oriented programming, and ARC do not fundamentally depend on any given OS, so the core computational language is neutral; the coupling appears mainly at the interop/runtime-library boundary (Objective-C bridging, Foundation) rather than in core syntax/semantics.

Micro benchmark programs use only core language features and Foundation, and would compile with the open-source Swift toolchain on Linux with at most minor conditional-import adjustments, supporting a moderate but not full platform-neutrality rating.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.score_rationale: Scored 55/100: the core type system/generics/ARC/concurrency model is platform-neutral in design, but first-class language surface (availability attributes, historic Objective-C interop assumptions, Apple-centric ABI stabilization) embeds platform-specific concerns into the language itself more than platform-neutral peers (e.g. Go, Rust), limiting the score to mid-range.
